title: The coach's chair
summary: Take on a parent as your debater, build their case file with them rather than for them, hand over the signposting you learned a year ago, then take the bench you would never have picked and find out from the inside whether it can be argued well.
materials: a folder or a stapled bundle of paper for the case file
index cards, one per point, and two pens of different colours
a parent who is willing to be your debater for the next four weeks

steps.title: The third chair
steps.body:
There are three chairs in this room and you have now sat in two of them.

The debater's chair you have had for a year. The judge's chair you took in week 1, and you found out there that the person deciding is doing a job of their own rather than watching somebody else's.

Today, the third one. The corner. You are a coach from this week, and the person you are coaching is a parent.

What a coach owns is not the words. A coach who writes the speech has produced a parrot, and a parrot loses the moment anything unexpected happens, which is at about the ninety second mark. What a coach owns is the board. From the corner you can see the whole thing, both sides at once, which is exactly what the person inside the fight cannot see, because they are busy fighting.

So your first job is a case file, and it has four parts.

One, the motion written out in full, with a circle round every word that is going to get fought over. Motions are won and lost on one word more often than on any argument.

Two, three points. Each one is a claim, then a reason beginning with the word because, then the evidence, then where the evidence came from. Same shape you have used all year.

Three, the other side's best point, written down in their words, put as strongly as they would put it. Not the weak version. If your debater cannot read it out and feel uncomfortable, it is not the best version yet. Then the answer to it underneath.

Four, the two questions your debater would least like to be asked, and what they say when those arrive. They will arrive.

And here is the part that makes it coaching. You build all four of those with them, not for them. Two pens of different colours, and their colour has to be on at least two of the four parts by the end. A case file written entirely in your handwriting is your case file. They will drop it in the first minute, because nobody defends somebody else's sentences.

Then hand over the signposting. You learned it a year ago and you barely notice it now: my first point, my second point, and after every claim, the words here is how I know. Teach it, then listen for it. The test of teaching is never whether you said it. It is whether they did it.

Last, the drill, and it is a strange one on purpose.

The motion is: arguing for a side you do not believe is a kind of lying. You are speaking for it.

Read that again. You have spent a year doing the thing that motion attacks, and today you are being asked to prosecute it. That is not a trick, it is the week's question with a bench under it. If you can build a real case for it, one that makes the room actually think, then you have argued well for a side you would never pick, and you found that out by doing it rather than by having an opinion about it. If you cannot, that is also an answer, and honestly it is the more interesting one.

One thing that is not allowed inside the round: saying I do not really think this. Not once, not as a joke, not with your eyebrows. Say it afterwards on the recording, as loudly as you like.

The question to carry into that recording: can you argue well for a side you would never pick?

steps.title: Build the case file, with them and not for them
steps.body:
Sit down beside your debater, not opposite them. Physically. It changes the conversation more than it should.

Twenty minutes, four parts, two colours of pen.

Start with the motion and the circled words, and ask them what they think each circled word means before you say what you think it means. You will find out immediately whether you are about to argue the same motion.

Then the three points, one index card each, in the shape you already own: claim, then because, then evidence, then where the evidence came from. Your job here is questions, not sentences. Why would somebody believe that? What would you say if they asked for an example? Where did that number come from? A coach who is talking more than half the time is writing a speech.

Then the other side's best point. This is the part people skip and it is the part that wins rounds. Write it in their words. Then read it out to your debater in a serious voice and watch their face. If they look comfortable, it is not strong enough yet and you write it again.

Then the two worst questions. Ask them out loud, unkindly, the way an opponent would. Let your debater flounder once, on purpose, before you help. The floundering is the point of a drill. It cannot happen for the first time in the round.

Then hand the timer over and let them deliver the whole thing standing, twice, while you sit in the corner and say nothing at all during it. Between the two runs you get thirty seconds of coaching, and you may say exactly two things. Two. Choosing which two is the entire skill, and it is the skill week 8 is going to test in front of a judge.

Afterwards, ask them one question and let them answer it properly: which of the two things I said was actually useful?
checklist: The case file has all four parts, and my debater's own pen colour is on at least two of them
Every point carries a claim, a because reason, evidence, and where that evidence came from
The other side's best point is written in their words, and my debater agreed out loud that it was the strong version
The two worst questions are written down with an answer under each, and I asked them out loud before I helped
My debater signposted their own speech without being prompted at least once, and I gave exactly two pieces of coaching between the runs

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record two things in one take, in this order. First, your two minute constructive for the motion that arguing for a side you do not believe is a kind of lying, standing, cards in hand, delivered straight, with no face and no wink and nothing that tells the room you do not mean it. Then stop, sit down, and answer this week's question: can you argue well for a side you would never pick, and what is your reason? Say whether building that case changed anything about what you think, and say which sentence in it was the hardest one to get out of your mouth. Finish with the two pieces of coaching you gave your debater and which of them they said was useful.
